extracted.intended_audience: folklorists, humor scholars, and students studying humor theory
extracted.subtask_description: Apply Elliott Oring's 'appropriate incongruity' refinement of incongruity theory to evaluate or produce humorous instances by identifying conflicting categories and the non-trivial dimension that makes their union feel fitting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate incongruity (defining formula)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor arises from the perception of an appropriate incongruity — that is, an incongruity that, when perceived, is recognized as in some sense fitting, apt, or meaningful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The comic experience requires holding both the 'incongruity moment' ('these don't go together') and the 'appropriateness moment' ('but they do, in this clever sense') simultaneously. This combination — perceived conflict plus perceived rightness — produces humor. Example forms: a pun (two senses joined), a metaphor (two domains joined), a caricature (distortion that still fits).

rubrics_metrics.name: A perceived incongruity
rubrics_metrics.description: There must be a perceived incongruity — categories, expectations, or frames in conflict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluator should identify which categories or frames are being set in opposition. Diagnostic question: 'What incongruity is being perceived?' Example: a pun juxtaposes different meanings; a metaphor juxtaposes different domains.

rubrics_metrics.name: A perceived appropriateness
rubrics_metrics.description: There must be a perceived appropriateness — a sense that the conflicting elements actually do connect on some non-obvious dimension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluator should specify the dimension along which the incongruous elements are nevertheless appropriate (the 'why it fits'). Diagnostic question: 'What is the appropriateness — the dimension on which the incongruous elements nevertheless connect?' Examples: same word sense, hidden similarity, exaggerated yet recognizable trait.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-triviality of the connection
rubrics_metrics.description: The connection between the incongruous elements must be non-trivial — it must be just barely discoverable; if it is too obvious there is no comic spike.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether the appropriateness is neither too easy nor impossible to find. Diagnostic question: 'Is the appropriateness non-trivial (not too easy, not impossible)?' Anti-pattern: an immediately obvious fit yields no humor; an inscrutable fit yields bewilderment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perceiver enjoyment of the held tension
rubrics_metrics.description: The perceiver must enjoy holding both the incongruity and the appropriateness simultaneously, not merely arrive at a sober understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish amusement from mere intellectual recognition. Diagnostic question: 'Does the audience enjoy the held tension, or does it resolve into mere understanding?' If the perceiver simply solves the puzzle without pleasure, the comic effect is absent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid pure incongruity (anti-patterns and alternate outcomes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Incongruity without perceived appropriateness produces non-comic reactions such as bewilderment, surprise, horror, or mystery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be alert for these outcomes when appropriateness is missing: 'Bewilderment' — no perceptible connection; 'Surprise' — incongruity resolves into a different ordinary frame; 'Horror' — connection via threatening dimension; 'Mystery' — possible appropriateness not yet perceived. These indicate failure to meet the appropriate-incongruity condition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid pure appropriateness without incongruity (anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: Appropriateness without any incongruity produces aesthetic recognition or insight rather than humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If elements fit neatly without conflict, the result is pleasure or understanding (aesthetic recognition/insight) but lacks the comic edge. Use this to rule out non-humorous parallels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnostic checklist for evaluating a candidate humor instance
rubrics_metrics.description: For a candidate humor instance, explicitly identify the incongruous categories, the dimension of appropriateness, the non-triviality of that appropriateness, and whether the perceiver enjoys holding both simultaneously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete steps: (1) What incongruity is being perceived? (2) What is the appropriateness — the connecting dimension? (3) Is the appropriateness non-trivial? (4) Does the audience enjoy the held tension? Use these questions as an evaluation rubric; the page's 'Diagnostic questions' map directly to these steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor as cultural commentary (contextual/cultural criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Appropriate incongruity often functions as cultural commentary, joining categories in ways that reveal social meanings or tensions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether the fit operates to comment on cultural categories (e.g., ethnic humor, joining sacred and profane, pretension vs. reality, cross-genre/internet meme juxtapositions). Evaluate how sociocultural contexts shape what counts as 'appropriate' and whether the humor's appropriateness implicates cultural norms or power relations.
